summary: Spawn is a hosted platform where people make multiplayer games and worlds by talking to a built-in AI builder, and play them in a web browser, a desktop app or on a phone. Underneath, every world is a git repository of Spawn's own object rows and JavaScript scripts, built on the three.js graphics library, and outside AI agents can create and change worlds through a published web interface and plain git without a person present. Within Spawn it covers a lot: GLB models and rigged GLB bodies that follow a player into every world, portals between any two Spawn worlds that carry held items, saved values and even running object scripts under the host world's limits, saved inventories, an in-game currency with platform-held purchase records, and version history. None of this reaches outside Spawn: addresses, accounts, the currency and portals work only between Spawn worlds, a copy of a world refers to its models by name instead of containing them, and Spawn's policy forbids using its builder to make games for other platforms. Two traps for a standards reader: player movement is trusted from each player's own machine rather than checked by a server, and the admission check on a portal runs on the arriving player's machine, so a modified client can skip it.

coverage.note: A world is a tree of objects written as one YAML row per object, with children nested under a parent and transforms that carry down to children. The format is Spawn's own; it borrows three.js shape names and material fields but is not a published interchange format.

coverage.note: A world's files and history are a git repository the owner can copy, and a game made elsewhere can be brought in by rewriting it for Spawn. Missing: a copy holds Spawn's own file layout and refers to models, images and sounds by name rather than carrying them, and Spawn provides no ready-to-run export for another engine or platform. Its use policy also forbids using its builder to make games for other platforms.
